observation.visible_scene: A three-tiered white snowman-like figure (stacked cotton/snow balls) centered against a textured yellow backdrop. The top sphere (head) wears a small green cylindrical cap; the middle sphere has two short side protrusions (arms) and a vertical line of blue dotted marks; the bottom sphere also carries a vertical line of blue dots. The figure rests on a clear glass tumbler, which sits on a white plate over a gray surface at the bottom of the frame. Lighting and background are uniform throughout.
visible_changes: The head sphere together with its green cap drifts steadily downward over the clip, so the green cap appears to sink into the top of the head and the head closes the gap toward the middle sphere (top tier descends relative to the body).
The middle sphere (and its arms) shifts slightly downward relative to the bottom sphere, indicating a gentle vertical compression/settling of the stack from the top down.

The bottom sphere, the glass, the plate, the gray floor line, and the yellow background remain in fixed positions, so the apparent motion is internal to the stacked figure rather than a camera pan; the camera looks static.
The blue dotted markings on each sphere keep their relative arrangement within each sphere (no lateral motion), only translating with their host sphere.
The change is slow, smooth and monotonic across the sampled frames; no sudden jump, contact event, or disappearance is visible.
outside_clip_unknowns: What caused the top to settle (compression, melting, sagging, or an unseen force) is not shown.
Whether the settling continues, stops, or reverses after the last frame is unknown.
The state before t=0 (whether the head was already descending) is not shown.
Material identity of the balls and cap is not confirmed by the clip.
uncertain_details: Exact pixel magnitudes of each tier's shift are approximate; the small downward drift of the middle sphere could partly be measurement noise versus real compression.
Whether there is any tiny camera drift versus a perfectly static camera cannot be fully resolved from the background alone.
The green cap's apparent sinking into the head may be partly a perspective/overlap effect of the head rising around it.
